overview: These two atlas records cover late medieval Sri Lanka from 1279 to 1530. Their near-island-wide outlines are regional umbrellas: they do not show one Sinhala-speaking state ruling every district throughout that time. Royal centers shifted through Yapahuwa, Kurunegala and Gampola, while Kotte became powerful in the fifteenth century and divided in 1521. The Tamil kingdom of Jaffna, hill-country rulers and local communities had distinct histories. The simplified coast even clips the modern Colombo, Galle and Jaffna points, although their connections matter to this history. This card joins the two consecutive map phases while keeping earlier Anuradhapura-era and later named-state records separate.

periods.title: Fortresses and shifting centers
periods.summary: The map opens during Yapahuwa’s short period as a royal center. After its loss to a Pandyan attack in the 1280s, political centers shifted; 1279 is not the founding of a single island-wide kingdom.

periods.title: Gampola-era foundations
periods.summary: A dated inscription records the establishment of Gadaladeniya in 1344. Endowments and skilled construction supported Buddhist institutions amid changing royal politics.

periods.title: Kotte becomes a major court
periods.summary: By the early fifteenth century, Kotte had become a royal capital. Parakramabahu VI’s reign is associated with its greatest political reach, but the atlas boundary is not a measure of permanent control.

periods.title: A new map label, continuing societies
periods.summary: The second atlas record begins in 1492 with much the same broad island outline. Its label changes from singular to plural without marking a documented founding or conquest.

periods.title: Partition and rival courts
periods.summary: Kotte’s division among three brothers in 1521 created competing centers at Kotte, Sitawaka and Raigama. The hill country remained another political arena.

items.text: Yapahuwa combined a high rock stronghold with walls, ramparts and moats below. Bhuvanaikabahu I made it a royal center in the late thirteenth century and housed the Buddha’s Tooth Relic there. Custody of that revered object helped support claims to kingship. A Pandyan attack in the 1280s carried the relic to South India, ending Yapahuwa’s brief prominence as a capital.

Yapahuwa’s ornamental stairway is still crowded with carved beings: mythical makaras, small supporting figures and dancers. Stoneworkers combined a practical ascent with an elaborate setting for royal and religious authority. Rock-cut cisterns collected rainwater elsewhere in the fortress. Reaching the top required legs; keeping people there also required a dependable water supply.

Kotte’s strength began with its landscape. Waterways and marshes around the Kolonna Oya and Diyawanna Oya helped protect the fortress associated with Alakeshwara. Proximity to Colombo linked the inland court with maritime commerce. The early fifteenth-century kingdom grew from this defended setting, rather than appearing fully formed across the whole island on one foundation day.

Royal family conflict reshaped the later map phase. In 1521, three brothers divided Kotte’s territories: Bhuvanaikabahu held Kotte, Mayadunne ruled from Sitawaka, and Raigam Bandara received Raigama. Their competing ambitions influenced alliances and war. Jaffna and the hill-country rulers cannot be folded into that family partition as if they were merely districts of an uncontested kingdom.

The Gadaladeniya inscription, dated 1344, names Dharmmakirtti as the founder and Ganesvaracari as the leading master artisan. It describes payments in money and paddy to craftspeople skilled in architecture and making images. The shrine’s South Indian connections are visible in its design and the architect’s name, although a name alone does not reveal every worker’s origin.

Temple donations could leave room for a donor’s family. Gadaladeniya’s long grant list includes Anura Attara’s land with a reservation allowing his relations to enjoy it while paying customary dues and tithes. Other gifts included a house and garden. Such clauses show how religious endowments intersected with continuing household livelihoods, rather than simply removing land from everyday use.

At nearby Lankatilaka, a 1344 inscription describes artisans receiving paddy, gold, silver and cloth for constructing the image-house. It also credits the minister’s sons and women of his household with a pavilion containing a bronze image. The record presents building as a collaboration involving rulers, officials, religious communities, craftspeople and an elite family.

The same foundation depended on unequal labor. Lankatilaka’s records list 200 enslaved men and women, some inherited or received through marriage and others purchased, alongside cattle and buffaloes. They also prescribe a small annual contribution from each household for offerings and ceremonies. The inscriptions praise generosity, but the people assigned as property could not choose freely how to work.

Lankatilaka’s land grants describe improving fields with a new dam, removing stumps and making embankments. Rice-producing land supported offerings, lamps, flowers and festivities at the shrine. The grand building therefore depended on less glamorous tasks beyond its walls: cultivating fields, tending animals and keeping water under control. The record does not establish plumbing or toilets in ordinary homes.

Around 1500, Colombo traded cinnamon, areca nuts, gems and elephants for imported goods including cloth and rice. The port was culturally and religiously diverse. Its exchange networks connected producers, carriers and traders with the royal economy at Kotte. Colombo lies just outside this particular simplified polygon, so its importance should not be mistaken for evidence that the drawn coastline is accurate.

A bird could deliver a very important message in Sinhala poetry. Around 1450, the monk Sri Rahula composed the Selalihini Sandeshaya, imagining a journey from Kotte to Kelaniya to ask a deity to grant a princess a son. Its author headed Vijayabahu Pirivena, a monastic learning institution. This was literary invention and royal aspiration, not a report of a working bird-post service.

The poem also describes women singing Tamil hymns at a Hindu shrine and female dancers at Kelaniya. Those scenes illuminate how a Sinhala Buddhist poet imagined public worship and performance. They cannot tell us what every woman was permitted to do, but they preserve a richer social picture than a list containing only kings and battles.

For a small Sinhala sample, verse 7 uses “සුරපුර,” glossed by translator Dharshani Lakmali Jayasinghe as “city of gods.” The poet compares Kotte with a celestial city. These are modern printed Sinhala letters representing a word in the fifteenth-century poem, not a photograph of an original medieval manuscript. The praise belongs to poetry, not a measured city ranking.

A very different written object was found at Galle in 1911: a stone bearing Chinese, Tamil and Persian texts and the date 1409. Brought by Zheng He’s expedition, it records religious offerings and is now in the Colombo National Museum. This foreign-sponsored inscription reveals Indian Ocean connections; it is not a Sinhala royal proclamation or proof that everyone spoke all three languages.

Portuguese influence did not arrive as complete territorial control. A fort and cinnamon trading post were established at Colombo in 1518, but the fort was dismantled in 1524. Bhuvanaikabahu later sought military support against Sitawaka. Trading arrangements, local rivalries and changing garrisons shaped the relationship long before direct colonial government replaced Kotte’s court.

Cinnamon profits encouraged attempts to control routes and supply. Historian C. R. de Silva describes a Portuguese Crown monopoly decision for the oceanic trade route in 1520 and a 1524 order directing cinnamon cargoes through Cochin. He also reports the destruction of surplus cinnamon to support prices. A fragrant ingredient could sit at the center of coercive commercial policy, far from the kitchens where it was used.

ending.text: Neither 1492 nor 1530 marks the disappearance of these communities. Kotte had already divided in 1521, and later conflict drove its court to Colombo in 1565. The Kotte royal line continued under Dharmapala until 1597, while other states and communities followed different paths. The map’s two intervals capture parts of that transition, not a single island-wide fall.
